activities.caption: call the magnitude — calibrate your joule sense
activities.name: ecJouleEstimate

config.prompt: A full smartphone charge stores roughly how many joules?
config.why: About 10,000 J — between lifting an apple one metre (≈1 J) and a chocolate bar (≈1,000,000 J), with a lightning bolt at ≈1,000,000,000 J.
config.context: At 1 J per apple-metre, a phone charge could lift a 100 g apple about 10 kilometres.

activities.anchor: most of which friction promptly converts to thermal energy in the floor.
activities.caption: find the faulty line — energy versus power
activities.name: ecPowerSpot

config.prompt: One line of this worked energy-and-power calculation is wrong. Find it.
lines: Climbing 3 m, a 60 kg student gains 60 × 9.8 × 3 ≈ 1,760 J.
Sprinting it in 5 s gives power = 1,760 J ÷ 5 s ≈ 350 W.
Walking it in 15 s gives the same energy at 1,760 ÷ 15 ≈ 117 W.
Energy and power are therefore the same quantity, measured over different times.
An electricity bill's kilowatt-hour is energy: 1 kW for 1 hour = 3,600,000 J.
config.correction: Energy is how much; power is how fast — 1,760 J delivered at 350 W or at 117 W is the same energy at different power.
config.why: Power divides energy by time; the joule and the watt measure different things.

activities.anchor: implementable anywhere the right causal organisation is realised.
activities.caption: slide between identity theory and functional role
activities.name: pomIdentityCompare

config.prompt: Slide between the two physicalist strategies for explaining pain.

before.label: Type identity theory
before.text: Mental states are identical to one neural type — pain is a specific brain state, discovered the way water was discovered to be H₂O.

after.label: Functionalism
after.text: Mental states are defined by causal role — typical inputs, relations to other states and outputs — so pain can run on a mammal, bird or octopus brain.

config.why: Multiple realisability is the objection that becomes functionalism's selling point: same organisation, different hardware.

config.root: A system produces fluent Chinese replies by shuffling symbols according to rules. Does it understand Chinese?

start.text: A man in a room follows a rulebook to produce perfect Chinese answers, without knowing a word of Chinese.

choices.label: No — following rules is syntax, not understanding
Yes — the whole room, not the man, is the understander

searle.text: Searle presses the point: even if the man memorises the rules, nothing in the room understands.

choices.label: Conclude that computation alone cannot produce understanding
choices.feedback: Strong AI is exactly what Searle denies.

choices.label: Ask whether biological embodiment is required
choices.feedback: This shifts the question from rules to the machine that runs them.

systems.text: The systems reply says understanding belongs to the whole organisation, not to any component.

choices.label: Ask what the system would need in order to be conscious
choices.feedback: This moves the debate to integration and unified subjects.

choices.label: Scale it up: does a large language model understand?
choices.feedback: The 1980 argument maps directly onto current AI debates.

strong-ai.text: Conclusion: symbol manipulation, however perfect, is not understanding — the strong-AI claim fails.

embodiment.text: The debate turns to embodiment: perhaps understanding needs a body, a world and causal contact, not just rules.

integration.text: The reply becomes that real minds are integrated, unified subjects — the missing integration is doing the explanatory work.

llm.text: The question returns at scale: is scale-plus-training understanding, or very good syntax? The argument reopens rather than closes.

config.why: The Chinese Room tests whether syntax can produce semantics; the systems reply shifts understanding to the whole organisation, and the debate is unresolved.
